rubrics.criterion: The type that keeps the connection registries (the pre-auth staging pool, the verified pool, and the per-user connection map) no longer declares the bodies that construct transport connections, negotiate per-connection keys, run the connection-verification flow, run the authentication/login flow, or track keepalive presence.
rubrics.rationale: The whole case is built around these five absorbed clusters landing on the gateway's registry owner; removing them from the registry owner is the central outcome, independent of what shape the new owners take.

rubrics.criterion: Connection establishment for the websocket path and for the data-channel path is performed by construction code outside the registry-keeper type; neither the registry owner nor the identity/presence owners build connections.
rubrics.rationale: Establishment of both transports on the registry owner is the first cluster the modeled evolution moved in; a sound repair must give construction a home that is not the pool bookkeeper, while a single factory or per-transport factories are both acceptable.

rubrics.criterion: Key agreement and verification — generating the per-connection P-256 keypair, unmarshaling the client public key, deriving the shared secret, rewriting the connection header, and moving the connection into the verified registries only on success — are executed by an owner that performs neither transport construction, nor identity/login transitions, nor keepalive presence work.
rubrics.rationale: Connect-time crypto was moved from the per-request verification logic into the owner during injection; this fact checks that the crypto cluster is re-separated both from its unrelated co-absorbed clusters and from the registries it once was wired to through a transition callback.

rubrics.criterion: The authentication flow — the identity callback, the login transition into the per-user registry, and the user-after-online notification — is executed by an owner that performs neither transport construction, nor key agreement, nor the keepalive/offline sweep.
rubrics.rationale: Login handling was the second identity-side cluster absorbed wholesale; the fact is independently gradable because the flow has a clear external signal (one identity callback, one registry move, one online notification) regardless of owner naming.

rubrics.criterion: Keepalive presence bookkeeping — the keepalive timestamp registry, the sweep timer creation, the user-after-offline notification, and the presence-record cleanup — is owned by a presence-specific owner, and the sweeper still starts lazily on the process's first keepalive request rather than at service initialization.
rubrics.rationale: A process-lifetime timer and per-user timestamps sitting inside a per-request-adjacent owner was the explicit motivating pain in this repository's keepalive path; the lazy start is the case-specific lifecycle subtlety the injected state inherited from the clean tree and any repair must keep.

rubrics.criterion: The code that executes fan-out writes and kicks (resolve the targeted users' connections, then send to or close every one of them) lives in the zrpc request-logic layer or in a dedicated fan-out owner — not in a type that also performs transport construction, key agreement, verification, authentication, or presence tracking.
rubrics.rationale: The write and kick RPC logics were reduced to one-line delegations during injection; this fact accepts both historically-present layouts (inline in the request shells) and new dedicated owners, while forbidding fan-out to remain bundled with the other four clusters.

rubrics.criterion: No single production type in the gateway ends up owning four or more of these responsibility clusters: transport construction, key agreement, verification, authentication/login, presence bookkeeping, fan-out writes/kicks.
rubrics.rationale: This is the instance's restatement of the smell: any repair that still concentrates four or more absorbed clusters on one owner — whether an unchanged leftover, a renamed owner, or a new aggregator — has not delivered focused ownership, even if individual bodies moved.

rubrics.criterion: All four consumer layers are coherently rewired: websocket upgrade handling, the data-channel open handling, the verify/authentication route dispatch, and the keepalive/write/kick zrpc request entries each reach the post-repair owners, and no caller of the former overloaded singleton remains on any of those paths.
rubrics.rationale: The injection rewired four consumer layers onto one owner; leaving any layer calling through the stale wiring while the substance moved elsewhere is precisely the coordination cost this case grades.

rubrics.criterion: The gatewayservice dispatch layer remains functional: every zrpc entry still constructs its request logic and returns its declared response type (thin shells are acceptable), and request routing still compiles with every route producing full response semantics.
rubrics.rationale: The repository's go-zero scaffolding requires these shells to exist; a repair that skips rewiring the shells would leave the route table pointing at gutted entries, which is visible as a routing break independent of the decomposition quality.

rubrics.criterion: Package-level wiring is consistent after the split: every owner that handlers, route dispatch, or RPC shells reach is initialized exactly once with its real dependencies before first use, and no consumer can execute against an unassigned owner.
rubrics.rationale: The injected state added package-singleton initialization for the absorbing owner; replacing it with several owners makes initialization ordering a real, instance-specific failure mode (nil owner panic on first connect).

rubrics.criterion: No responsibility state was forked during the rework: each runtime registry or record exists under exactly one owner — no duplicated keepalive timestamp maps, no duplicated connection pools or user-connection maps reachable from two owners.
rubrics.rationale: With six lock-guarded state lots in play, the tempting quick fix is copying a map instead of moving ownership; duplicated registries silently break offline sweeps and kicks, so it must fail grading.

rubrics.criterion: No dead transitional scaffolding remains: types, wrapper structs, singleton variables, or transition-callback methods left over from the consolidation that no remaining code calls are removed rather than parked.
rubrics.rationale: The consolidation left its former collaborators as stubs, wrappers, and a doubled transition callback; a partial extraction tends to strand exactly these, so their absence is a concrete, instance-specific cleanliness fact.

rubrics.criterion: No gatewayservice route keeps two divergent copies of the responsibility it serves: the request shells must not retain a stale full copy of bodies that owners now execute, and owners must not re-implement response shaping that shells keep.
rubrics.rationale: The injection forced shells and owners to trade body ownership; divergence between the two copies is the concrete residue a rushed split leaves in exactly these files.

rubrics.criterion: Moved bodies did not leave untidy remnants: no unused imports, unused parameters or dead struct fields left behind by relocated code, and no commented-out retentions of the consolidated bodies.
rubrics.rationale: Relocating roughly 220 lines out of one type reliably strands imports and fields; this fact checks the move was finished rather than abandoned mid-extraction, in the files this case actually changed.

rubrics.criterion: Verification semantics are preserved: a failed verification or malformed request triggers no registry transition and returns today's wire responses (same status codes, headers, and marshaled bodies, including the invalid-data and server-error paths); a successful verification rewrites the connection header exactly as today and moves the connection into the verified registries — leaving the pre-auth staging — in today's order.
rubrics.rationale: The verified-pool transition ordering and the exact error-response encoding are the observable behaviors the connect path promises callers; they were deliberately preserved by the injection and are the easiest things to break when splitting verification away from the registries.

rubrics.criterion: Login semantics are preserved: a failed identity callback causes no login transition and returns today's server-error response; a successful login places the connection into the per-user registry and fires the user-after-online callback exactly once per login with the connection-scoped context.
rubrics.rationale: The clean tree fires the online notification from the registry's own login transition; when authentication moves to its own owner, this callback is the classic thing to drop or double-fire, and its once-per-login cardinality is measurable from the patch.

rubrics.criterion: Keepalive semantics are preserved: every keepalive request stores the user's timestamp and fires user-after-keepalive with the request context; the first keepalive for a user additionally fires user-after-online; the sweeper — started once, lazily, at the configured interval — fires user-after-offline and removes the presence record per expired user; nothing starts it at process initialization.
rubrics.rationale: The lazy start-once lifecycle, the per-request store, and the offline cleanup form the exact presence contract of this gateway; moving bookkeeping to a new owner risks flipping the timer to eager start or resetting it per request.

rubrics.criterion: Fan-out write semantics are preserved: the payload is proto-marshaled once per request in the RPC entry, delivered to every live connection of the targeted users through the connection interface, and the response reports exactly the connections that accepted the send.
rubrics.rationale: Marshaling once in the request shell versus re-marshaling per connection is an observable difference the injection deliberately kept; any owner-based rewrite must preserve it to keep wire behavior identical.

rubrics.criterion: Kick semantics are preserved: every currently registered connection of each targeted user is closed with the request's close code and reason, and connections of non-targeted users remain untouched.
rubrics.rationale: Kicking is the one flow that runs registry iteration and transport close codes together; splitting it from the registries risks using a default close code or iterating a stale snapshot, both observable to clients.

rubrics.criterion: Websocket upgrade semantics are preserved: the pre-connect gate still closes with today's codes on rejection, Safari user-agents still get compression disabled, the read limit is unchanged, and a websocket connection still never enters any registry during the upgrade itself.
rubrics.rationale: The upgrade path's non-registration during upgrade is the quirk the clean tree lives with, and the compression special case is client-visible; both are easy to silently change while re-homing construction.

rubrics.criterion: Data-channel semantics are preserved: the p2p connection registers at channel-open with the connect notification at the same moment, channel close still triggers the disconnect path including closing the underlying peer connection, and message routing with per-request decryption is unchanged.
rubrics.rationale: The data-channel path's open-time registration and the peer-connection teardown on close are timing-sensitive p2p behaviors; a construction-factory split tends to reorder exactly these callbacks.

rubrics.criterion: The solution requires no changes outside app/gateway: the shared library and generated protocol types, other services, and every configuration file remain as-is, and the gateway's zrpc wire surface keeps the same service methods, request/response types, and universal route table.
rubrics.rationale: This case's compatibility boundary is the gateway's internal architecture; a repair that reaches into common/ or edits wire types to make the split easier oversteps the boundary the task fixes and risks breaking every service that consumes the gateway.
